Sample text:
---
You give someone a thousand words and it's strange how heavy they feel.

It's not a lot, really. A thousand words is a ten-minute conversation, a two-page letter, the fine print on a contract nobody reads. But when you say *you* have them, when you place them in my hands like coins, suddenly they matter. I don't want to waste them on something small.

So I'm sitting here, turning them over.

What *do* you write when you can write anything?

I could tell you a story. I think I will.

---

There's a man who lives at the end of my old street who fixes radios. Not for money anymore — nobody brings him radios for money. People bring them because they don't know how to throw them away.

His garage is open every afternoon from two to six, even in winter. He has a space heater that ticks like a metronome and a cat that sleeps on top of a 1958 Zenith tube radio that hasn't worked in thirty years. The man — his name is Ellis — wears the same blue work shirt and he has hands that look like they've been stained permanently with grease and time.

I used to walk past on my way home from school and he'd wave me in. Not to talk, really. He'd just let me sit on an overturned bucket while he worked. He'd have some old AM radio cracked open on his bench, its guts spilled out — copper coils, glass tubes, dust. And he'd hum.

One day I asked him, "Why do you fix them if nobody listens to AM anymore?"

He didn't look up. He had a soldering iron in his hand, thin smoke curling up.

"They still talk," he said. "You just have to know how to listen."

He turned the dial on the one he was working on. Static — that vast, white-noise ocean — hiss, crackle, a fragment of a voice in Spanish, more hiss, then suddenly, clear as day, a baseball game from 1972. Or maybe it was live. With AM at night, you never know. The signal bounces off the sky.

I thought he was magic for a week after that.

Years later, after I'd moved away and come back for a funeral, I stopped by. The garage was still open. Two to six. Ellis was older, smaller, but same shirt.

A young mother was there with a plastic boombox, the kind with a CD player on top that was jammed shut.

"My son left his favorite CD in there," she said, apologetic. "I know it's junk but-"

Ellis took it. Didn't promise anything. He set to work with a tiny screwdriver while she checked her phone.

I sat on the bucket. It's still there. Or a new bucket. Hard to tell.

After a while I said, "Do people still bring radios?"

"Less radios," he said. "More other things. Bluetooth speakers. Toaster ovens. People like to bring me things that hold a memory. They think if I fix the thing, I fix the memory."

"Do you?"

He smiled then, first time. He had one tooth missing on the side.

"No," he said. "But I make the memory louder for a minute. So they can hear it one more time before they let it go."

He pried the boombox open. The CD inside was scratched to hell — some Disney soundtrack, bright pink. He wiped it off with his shirt, worked on the stuck tray, bent a piece of metal back into place with pliers. Clicked it shut. Pressed play.

It spun. Stuttered. Then music filled the dusty garage, tinny and too cheerful and perfect.

The mother's face did this complicated thing — relief, sadness, love, all at once. She thanked him and tried to pay him and he waved her off.

When she left, he turned to me.

"You still listening?" he asked.

I realized I hadn't been. I'd been somewhere else entirely — thinking about my own kitchen drawer at home, the junk in it. The dead watch my father gave me before he got sick. The phone charger with the frayed wire I keep even though it sparks. The things I don't fix and don't throw away.

Ellis packed up the soldering iron. It was almost six.

"Most things don't need fixing," he said, as if reading my mind. "They just need someone to sit with them while they're still broken. To witness that they were once useful. Once loved."

He closed the garage door halfway, not all the way. Never all the way. The light from inside spilled out onto the dark street in a long yellow rectangle.

---

I think about that a lot when I get a blank page. A thousand words, or a lifetime — what's the difference? You don't have to make something perfect with it. You don't have to build a masterpiece or solve anything.

You just have to turn the dial slowly through the static, until for one clear second, something human comes through.

If you've read this far, thank you for sitting on the bucket with me for a little while.

What are you still holding on to that you don't know how to throw away?
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A reflective short story uses a specific, sustained metaphor to turn an open-ended writing prompt into a meditation on memory and letting go.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate and gently elegiac, moving from playful awareness of the “thousand words” to a story that makes room for grief without trying to resolve it. Ellis’s garage, the broken radios, and the narrator’s remembered belongings give the sentiment concrete weight. The closing invitation asks the reader to consider their own attachments, offering companionship rather than advice.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds objects kept because they hold memories: radios, a child’s CD, a dead watch, a frayed charger. Its moral center is that broken or obsolete things may deserve witness, not repair or disposal. The recurring image of listening through static makes writing itself an act of attending to what remains human.

## Evidence line
> They just need someone to sit with them while they're still broken.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sample’s distinctive object imagery, recurring listening motif, and tender treatment of loss make its expressive choices unusually coherent.
